title: Cracking Nature's Code: The Missing Enzymes Behind a Rare Cancer-Fighting Compound
summary: Deep inside tropical trees like kratom and cat's claw, a rare chemical called mitraphylline is produced in trace amounts. This compound belongs to a class of molecules known as spirooxindole alkaloids, prized for their unusual twisted ring structures and potent biological effects — including anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor activity. But there's a catch: mitraphylline is so scarce that extracting it from plants is impractical, and chemists couldn't synthesize it in the lab because they didn't know how nature does it. That mystery has now been solved. Researchers at UBC Okanagan, led by Dr. Thu-Thuy Dang and doctoral student Tuan-Anh Nguyen, have uncovered the two critical enzymes that plants use to assemble mitraphylline. The first enzyme organizes the molecule into its correct three-dimensional shape, while the second transforms it into mitraphylline itself. "This is similar to finding the missing links in an assembly line," Dr. Dang explained. "It answers a long-standing question about how nature builds these complex molecules and gives us a new way to replicate that process." The breakthrough builds on the team's 2023 discovery of the first plant enzyme capable of twisting a molecule into the distinctive spiro shape. Now, with the full biosynthetic pathway revealed, scientists have a clear path toward producing mitraphylline and related compounds in a sustainable, "green chemistry" way. Instead of relying on harsh chemicals or mining rare plants, they can use the enzymes as biological factories. Nguyen, who led the new research, emphasized the collaborative environment at UBC Okanagan. "Being part of the team that uncovered the enzymes behind spirooxindole compounds has been amazing," he said. The project involved international collaboration with Dr. Satya Nadakuduti's group at the University of Florida and was supported by Canadian and U.S. funding agencies. Mitraphylline's potential is enormous. Many promising natural compounds never become medicines because they're too hard to obtain. By harnessing the plant's own molecular tools, researchers can now explore a wider range of therapeutic compounds. "Plants are fantastic natural chemists," Dr. Dang said. "Our next steps will focus on adapting their molecular tools to create a wider range of therapeutic compounds." This discovery is a big win for green chemistry and could accelerate the development of new cancer treatments derived from nature's own playbook.
why_it_matters: Unlocking nature's assembly line for rare cancer-fighters could lead to affordable, sustainable production of new medicines that previously couldn't leave the lab. It promises to transform how we develop cancer therapies while protecting fragile ecosystems from the overharvesting of medicinal plants.

background_read: Many life-saving medicines, from aspirin (originally from willow bark) to the cancer drug paclitaxel (from the Pacific yew tree), started as plant compounds. Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is a tree native to Southeast Asia, known for its stimulant and pain-relieving effects, and its chemical relative mitraphylline has shown anti-tumor potential in early studies.

Cat's claw (Uncaria tomentosa) is a woody vine from the Amazon rainforest that Indigenous peoples have used for centuries to treat inflammation and wounds. Both plants produce spirooxindole alkaloids, molecules with a unique twisted core that makes them incredibly hard to recreate artificially in a lab.

Green chemistry, a philosophy promoted by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency since the 1990s, aims to design chemical processes that reduce waste and avoid toxic solvents. Using enzyme-based 'biological factories' fits perfectly with this approach, offering a sustainable alternative to harsh industrial synthesis.

The team at UBC Okanagan, led by natural products chemist Dr. Thu-Thuy Dang, collaborated with Dr. Satya Nadakuduti's group at the University of Florida, combining expertise in plant biochemistry and synthetic biology to crack the code of how nature builds these promising compounds.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — for pharmaceutical development and conservation
perspectives.description: This opens a way to produce mitraphylline and similar compounds in large quantities without stripping rare plants from the wild. It could accelerate the development of new cancer treatments and bring previously unavailable natural products into clinical use at lower cost and environmental impact.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / Critical — for a realistic view of drug development
perspectives.description: Many natural compounds that show anti-tumor activity in early tests fail later in expensive clinical trials. Even with the enzymes in hand, scaling up production to industrial levels can take a decade or more, and the enzyme-based process may not yet be efficient enough to compete with synthetic alternatives.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / Analytical — on the trend of biomimicry in chemistry
perspectives.description: This work reflects a broader shift in chemistry toward biomimicry — using nature's own catalysts instead of brute-force synthetic chemistry. By understanding biosynthetic pathways, scientists are increasingly able to tweak and redirect plant enzymes to create novel drug candidates that nature never evolved.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — toward a library of new cancer drugs
perspectives.description: The team plans to engineer these enzymes to produce a whole family of spirooxindole alkaloids. If they can partner with pharmaceutical companies and overcome scale-up challenges, we could see the first mitraphylline-inspired drugs enter clinical trials within the next decade, potentially giving doctors a new class of plant-derived cancer therapies.
